title: QuickBooks Chart of Accounts Cleanup Is Live: Tie Out the Trial Balance by Period, Map Old and New Accounts to the Firm Standard, and Approve Each Cleanup Session per Client Before the Prior-Year Comparison Breaks
excerpt: Intuit's November 16, 2026 accountant release notes put QuickBooks chart of accounts cleanup in every QuickBooks Online plan: Intuit Intelligence proposes merges, groupings, inactivations, renames, and type changes, and nothing changes until you approve. The help article adds the two facts that decide how a firm should use it: approved changes can't be undone, and by default transactions before the closed books date stay in the old account. Here is the per-period trial balance tie-out, the old-to-new account map, and the approval order a firm should run on one client before onboarding the next 50.

content:
QuickBooks chart of accounts cleanup is live. Intuit Intelligence proposes merges, groupings, inactivations, renames, and type changes in a client's file, and you approve each one. Before a firm runs it, tie out the trial balance by period, map old and kept accounts to the firm standard line, and fix the approval order, because approved changes can't be undone.

Why QuickBooks chart of accounts cleanup needs a firm standard now

Intuit's help article Clean up your chart of accounts in QuickBooks Online, updated 2026-11-10, describes a cleanup session with five tabs: Consolidate, Duplicates, Inactive, Rename, and Change type. The tool 'uses Intuit Intelligence to find these issues and suggest fixes,' and nothing changes until you approve each suggestion. It is available in Simple Start, Essentials, Plus, and Advanced, and 'some recommendations are only available to accountants.' Three sentences in that article decide how a firm should use it. First: 'You can't undo changes after you approve them.' Second: 'By default, Chart of Accounts Cleanup respects your closed books date and won't make changes to any transactions before it.' Third, on what a merge does: 'QuickBooks reclassifies the transactions from that time period into the account you keep,' while 'earlier transactions stay in the inactive account, so financial reports you've already filed don't change.'

Intuit's accountant channel put the feature in front of firms in its November 2026 release notes, published 2026-11-16, under the heading 'Clean up client books faster with Chart of Accounts cleanup.' The pitch is new-client onboarding: the tool 'uses Intuit Intelligence to find common problems in a new client's chart of accounts and helps you correct the issues,' replacing the 'repetitive, cumbersome, and manual work' of rearranging accounts and reclassifying transactions. The same release adds firm-side Bill Pay approval workflows that 'let you define more approvers for a client's bill payments,' and it follows the AI reconciliation release by a week. Intuit is handing firms more automation per client file, each piece with its own approval step, and none of them with a firm-wide standard attached.

The closed-books default is the part that changes the accounting. Intuit's article on merging duplicate accounts, updated 2026-09-01, describes the standard merge: 'The merge moves all past transactions into the account you keep and makes the duplicate account inactive,' both accounts must share the same name, type, and detail type, accounts connected to online banking can't be merged, and 'merging is permanent and can't be undone.' The lock your books article, updated 2026-09-15, explains the other half: once a closing date is set, 'you can't change any transactions on or before that date without approval,' with a warning or a warning plus a password. Put the two together and the cleanup tool does something the standard merge never did. It splits one economic account into two ledger accounts at the closing date: the old account keeps the history, the kept account takes the future.

Coverage outside Intuit doesn't address that split. A comparison of QuickBooks Online, Keeper, and Dext for chart standardization, dated 2026-05-22, builds a master template and a governance workflow and tells firms to reclassify historical transactions so reports stay comparable. A cleanup checklist from 2026-08-10 shows how an 89-account chart becomes 34 accounts by designing around how the business operates. Both are useful on design. Neither covers the new tool, what the closed-books default does to a prior-year comparison, or how to prove the trial balance didn't move. That's what this article covers.

What each cleanup action does to the ledger, and what it does to the comparison

Start from what a trial balance proves. Every account carries a normal balance by type: assets and expenses debit; liabilities, equity, and income credit. A merge between two accounts of the same type moves debits and credits from one line to another inside the same statement section. Total debits still equal total credits, every subtotal is unchanged, and net income for each period is unchanged. A merge changes detail, not results. The Duplicates and Consolidate tabs live here, as long as the two accounts really are the same type and detail type.

A type change is different. Moving an account from Expense to Cost of Goods Sold leaves net income alone and changes gross profit for every period the account has activity. Moving an account from Expense to Other Expense changes operating income. Moving an account from an income statement type to a balance sheet type, say from Repairs to Fixed Assets, changes net income, retained earnings, and total assets at the same time, because a flow item becomes a point-in-time item. The help article says Change type 'shows accounts that may have the wrong type, and may even show up on the wrong financial statement,' and that QuickBooks 'suggests a new account type and detail type.' It doesn't say whether the closed-books protection applies to a type change, so a firm has to find out by running the prior-year statements before and after on one account.

Now the comparison. Suppose a client's 2025 books are closed and the cleanup merges 'Meals - Client' into 'Meals and Entertainment' in November 2026. Transactions dated 2026 move to the kept account. Transactions dated 2025 stay in 'Meals - Client,' which is now inactive. The year-over-year profit and loss in QuickBooks shows 'Meals - Client' at $7,100 for January to October 2025 and $0 for the same months of 2026, a 100 percent decrease, and 'Meals and Entertainment' at $3,100 against $12,900, a 316 percent increase. Both lines are arithmetically right and both are useless to the client. The firm's standard line 'Meals' maps both accounts to one row and reads $10,200 against $12,900, up 26 percent. That is the number the client should see, and it exists only if the firm keeps a mapping layer that holds old and new accounts together instead of relying on the ledger's own account list.

One firm, one new client, one cleanup session: the walk-through

Call the firm Harbor Row Accounting: 48 QuickBooks Online client files, a standard chart of 96 lines that every client maps to, five bookkeepers, two reviewers, one engagement partner. The new client is Pine and Vale Cabinetry LLC, onboarded in November 2026 with 214 accounts, a closing date of December 31, 2025 with a password, and a filed 2025 return. The cleanup session proposes 115 changes: 23 duplicate merges, 11 consolidations, 58 inactivations, 17 renames, and 6 type changes. The figures are illustrative; the sequence is the point.

Step one: export the baseline before opening the cleanup

The bookkeeper exports the chart of accounts with type, detail type, and balance, then the trial balance at December 31, 2025 and at each month end from January through October 2026, the profit and loss for January to October 2026 with the prior-year column, and the balance sheet at December 31, 2025 and October 31, 2026. The baseline figures: net income of $186,420.00 for January to October 2026, gross profit of $412,300.00, and total assets of $1,284,650.00 at October 31, 2026. The file notes the closing date, the security setting, and which accounts carry a bank connection. Without this export the firm can only say the cleanup looked fine.

Step two: build the account map and classify every suggestion

Each of the 115 suggestions gets a row: old account, kept account, old type and detail type, kept type and detail type, firm standard line, and a class. The classes are the five in the table. Three of the 23 duplicate suggestions pair accounts of different detail types; one would merge a vehicle loan into a credit card. Those are rejected on sight. Four of the 58 inactivation candidates carry balances at some period end, including 'Deposits Held' at $2,250.00, so they stay active. Two consolidations would group a cost of goods sold account under an expense parent and are rejected. The six type changes are set aside for the partner.

Step three: approve in order and tie out after each batch

Renames go first, because they move nothing. Then same-type merges, then consolidations, then inactivations. After each batch the reviewer reruns the trial balance at December 31, 2025 and October 31, 2026 and the monthly net income for 2026 and compares them to the baseline to the cent. Any difference stops the session. Through four batches, net income, gross profit, and total assets are unchanged, which is what a same-type merge should produce. The time: 2 hours 50 minutes of bookkeeper time and 1 hour 30 minutes of review, against 6 hours 40 minutes and 1 hour 15 minutes for a comparable manual cleanup in September. The saving is real, and about half of it was spent on tie-outs the manual process never had.

Step four: rebuild the comparison through the map

The 'Meals - Client' merge from the previous section is one of the 23. In the QuickBooks comparison it reads as a 100 percent decrease on one line and a 316 percent increase on another. In the firm's mapped profit and loss, 'Meals' reads $10,200 against $12,900. The reviewer runs the same check on every merged pair: the mapped prior-year total equals the sum of the old and kept accounts' prior-year balances, and the mapped current-year total equals the kept account's current-year balance. Sixteen of the 23 merges have prior-year activity, so sixteen standard lines need both accounts mapped. A firm that delivers consolidated reports across 50 clients already owns this map; the cleanup session just adds rows to it.

Step five: decide what the closed year keeps, and record it

The partner reviews the six type changes. 'Subcontract Labor,' $96,500.00 for January to October 2026, is suggested as Cost of Goods Sold instead of Expense. Approving it moves gross profit from $412,300.00 to $315,800.00 and leaves net income at $186,420.00. The reviewer approves it on that one account first and reruns the 2025 profit and loss. If 2025 gross profit also moved, the type change reached behind the closing date, and the firm records a restated prior-year comparative and checks the 2025 return workpaper, where the amount sat on an expense line. The partner approves four type changes, rejects two, and signs the cleanup register for the client. The closed year keeps its detail; the map carries the comparability. For firms that provide outsourced accounting services, that register is the document the next reviewer reads when staff change.

Accounting controls for QuickBooks chart of accounts cleanup

Source data: the chart of accounts export with account type, detail type, and balance taken before the session; the trial balance at the closing date and at every month end in the open year; the profit and loss with its prior-year column and the balance sheet at both dates; the closing date and security setting; the list of bank-connected accounts; the cleanup suggestion list with each disposition; the Audit Log entries for the session; and the dated Intuit pages the firm relied on, including the help article updated 2026-11-10 and the release notes published 2026-11-16. Record the plan tier and whether accountant-only tabs were visible, because availability varies.

Calculation: a fixed sequence anyone can rerun. Total debits equal total credits on every trial balance before and after. For same-type merges, net income by month, gross profit, operating income, and total assets after the batch equal the baseline to the cent. For each merged pair, the mapped prior-year total equals the old account's prior-year balance plus the kept account's prior-year balance, and the mapped current-year total equals the kept account's current-year balance. For each type change, the expected movement is stated in advance: a move into Cost of Goods Sold reduces gross profit by the account's period balance and leaves net income unchanged; a move across statements changes net income and equity by the same amount. For each inactivation, the balance at every period end equals zero. Polarity is preserved throughout: an expense account carries a debit balance, and moving it to an income type presents it as negative income without changing net income.

Review: a second person, not the bookkeeper who approved the suggestions, reruns the tie-out after each batch, confirms every rejected duplicate had a different detail type or a bank connection, confirms every inactivated account had a zero balance at every period end, confirms the mapping file and tax-line crosswalk carry both the old and kept accounts, runs the prior-year statements before and after the first type change, and signs the cleanup register before the next batch opens. Any unexplained difference stops the session.

Decision: the engagement partner owns the approval of type changes and of any change that reaches behind the closing date. The reviewer owns the sign-off on each batch. The bookkeeper owns the disposition of each suggestion and the register. The firm's standard chart owner decides which kept account names match the standard, so a cleanup on one client doesn't invent a name the other 47 don't use. The client's Primary Admin should be told, in writing, that approved changes can't be undone and that the firm runs cleanup sessions, not the client.

Limits and common mistakes

Intuit has not published the rules Intuit Intelligence uses to pair accounts or to suggest a type, and the help article doesn't say whether the closed-books default applies to type changes or can be switched off. The sequence above is a firm's own policy, not an Intuit specification, and it should be revisited when the product changes.

Don't approve a merge because the names look alike. A duplicate suggestion between a loan and a credit card, or between a Cost of Goods Sold account and an Expense account, is a type change wearing a merge label.

Don't read the ledger's year-over-year report after a cleanup and call the variance performance. The split at the closing date is a presentation effect. The mapped report is the one the client should see.

Don't inactivate an account with a balance. QuickBooks warns when an account being inactivated still carries one; the reviewer checks every period end, not just today's.

Don't run the cleanup on a client whose closing date was never set. Without a closing date the tool has nothing to respect, and a merge reaches all the way back through filed years.

Don't skip the baseline export because the session looks small. A 115-suggestion session on a 214-account chart took under three hours; the tie-out is what made it defensible.

Harbor Row Accounting, Pine and Vale Cabinetry LLC, and their figures are illustrative. The feature descriptions, dates, defaults, and undo behavior come from the Intuit pages cited above. Plan availability and accountant-only tabs vary by subscription and role.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does QuickBooks chart of accounts cleanup change in a client's books?

According to Intuit's help article updated November 10, 2026, a cleanup session proposes changes in five tabs: Consolidate, Duplicates, Inactive, Rename, and Change type. Nothing changes until you approve each suggestion, and approved changes can't be undone. When accounts merge, QuickBooks reclassifies transactions after the closed books date into the account you keep, and earlier transactions stay in the inactive account.

Does the cleanup tool change financial reports a firm has already filed?

By default it does not. Intuit states that the tool respects the closed books date and won't make changes to any transactions before it, so filed reports keep their detail. The help article does not say whether that protection applies to a type change, so a firm should run the prior-year statements before and after approving one type change on one account before approving the rest.

Why does the prior-year comparison break after a cleanup merge, and how is it fixed?

Because transactions before the closing date stay in the old account and transactions after it move to the kept account, the ledger's year-over-year report shows the old account falling to zero and the kept account rising by the reclassified amount. The fix is a mapping layer that maps both accounts to one standard reporting line, so the prior-year total is the sum of both accounts and the current-year total is the kept account.

Which cleanup suggestions change net income or gross profit?

Same-type merges, consolidations, renames, and zero-balance inactivations change none of them. A type change between sections of the same statement, such as Expense to Cost of Goods Sold, changes gross profit or operating income and leaves net income unchanged. A type change between statements, such as an expense account becoming a fixed asset, changes net income, retained earnings, and total assets by the same amount.

How should an accounting firm test chart of accounts cleanup before running it on every client?

Pick one new client with a closing date set and a filed prior-year return. Export the chart, the trial balance at the closing date and each month end, and the comparative statements. Classify every suggestion, approve renames first, then same-type merges, consolidations, and inactivations, and rerun the trial balance after each batch. Hold type changes for partner approval and test one before the rest. Record every disposition in a cleanup register and map old and kept accounts to the firm standard line.

Once every client's cleanup follows one approval order, one tie-out, and one map, the firm can see which files have been cleaned, which standard lines still carry unmapped accounts, and whether any client's gross profit moved during a session, across all 48 clients, before the month-end review rather than after. FinBoard maps every client's QuickBooks Online accounts to one standard chart, holds old and kept accounts on the same reporting line, and lets a reviewer drill from a mapped variance to the transactions behind it.
